name: Learning cycle
distinct: The minimal experience-before-vocabulary sequence, and the ancestor of 5E.
fit: Short concept sequences built on a clear lab phenomenon.
teacher: Designs the exploration, then introduces terms at the moment students need them.
learner: Explores, attaches new terms to experience, then applies them.
pitfall: Introducing terms before exploration, which collapses it into a traditional lesson.
evidence: Early studies (for example, Abraham & Renner, 1986) supported the sequence; it is included in 3E/5E/7E meta-analyses.

name: 7E
distinct: Separates eliciting prior knowledge from engaging interest, and adds far transfer.
fit: Topics with robust misconceptions and clear real-world transfer, such as Energy and Disease.
teacher: Diagnoses prior knowledge deliberately and designs a far-transfer task.
learner: Surfaces their own ideas and extends learning to unfamiliar contexts.
pitfall: Treating Elicit as a quick brainstorm whose results are never used.
evidence: Pooled with 5E in meta-analyses; the added phases rest on strong prior-knowledge and transfer research.

name: Generative Learning Model
phases: Challenge: compare with peers’ and scientists’ views
distinct: Makes the challenge between student and scientific views the centrepiece.
fit: Stubborn intuitive ideas: forces and motion, plant nutrition, heat and temperature.
teacher: Investigates students’ ideas first, then stages a respectful challenge.
learner: Clarifies, defends and revises their view against evidence.
pitfall: A ‘challenge’ that is really a correction, so students defer rather than reason.
evidence: Developed through the New Zealand Learning in Science Project; evidence is mainly classroom-based and qualitative.

name: CASE (Thinking Science)
distinct: Targets general reasoning patterns (control of variables, proportionality, probability, classification) rather than topic content.
fit: Stage 4 reasoning foundations that underpin planning (WS-03) and analysis (WS-06).
teacher: Manages conflict and group talk, withholds answers, and prompts reflection and bridging.
learner: Reasons aloud, reflects on how they thought, and transfers the pattern.
pitfall: Rushing to the right answer, which removes the conflict the lesson depends on.
evidence: Early UK studies reported lasting gains; a later large UK trial of the Let’s Think programme found no attainment effect, so implementation quality matters.

name: Interactive Approach
distinct: Students’ own questions drive the investigations.
fit: Local environments, Living systems and depth studies.
teacher: Elicits and sorts students’ questions, helping them become investigable.
learner: Generates questions and designs investigations to answer them.
pitfall: Collecting students’ questions and then answering them by lecture.
evidence: Originated in primary science; evidence is mainly classroom-based and qualitative.

name: Levels of inquiry
phases: Confirmation: question, method and answer given
Open: students pose question and method
distinct: Not a sequence but a way to calibrate how much the teacher specifies.
fit: Any practical work; plan a progression from Stage 4 to Stage 5.
teacher: Decides what to specify and fades support deliberately.
learner: Takes more design responsibility as the level rises.
pitfall: Jumping to open inquiry with novices, or never moving beyond confirmation.
evidence: A planning framework rather than a tested model; consistent with evidence that guided inquiry outperforms unguided discovery.

name: Argument-Driven Inquiry
distinct: Argument and peer critique are built into the investigation itself.
fit: Stage 5 investigations targeting SC5-WS-08; Reactions, Waves and motion.
teacher: Frames the guiding question and runs argumentation and peer review.
learner: Builds, critiques and revises arguments from evidence.
pitfall: Dropping the argumentation session or peer review when time runs short, which removes the core.
evidence: Quasi-experimental studies report gains in argument writing and science proficiency.

name: Science Writing Heuristic
distinct: A writing-to-learn scaffold that turns lab reports into reasoning.
fit: Any practical; particularly strong in EAL/D-rich classes. Builds WS-06 and WS-08.
teacher: Negotiates meaning in discussion and prompts comparison with the literature.
learner: Writes questions, claims and evidence, and reflects on how their thinking changed.
pitfall: Using the template as a fill-in form without the class negotiation of claims.
evidence: Multiple studies report gains, often largest for lower-achieving students.

name: Ambitious Science Teaching
distinct: Students’ explanatory models are drafted early and revised publicly across the unit.
fit: Unobservable mechanisms: particles, cells, genetics, climate, disease transmission.
teacher: Selects the anchoring phenomenon, then tracks and presses on students’ models.
learner: Drafts, tests and revises explanatory models in public.
pitfall: An anchoring phenomenon too thin to sustain a unit, or models that are never revised.
evidence: A growing body of classroom and design-based research; fewer controlled trials.

name: Problem-based learning
phases: What we know and need to know
distinct: The problem comes first; content is learned in order to solve it.
fit: Environmental sustainability, Disease, Materials; best with experienced learners.
teacher: Tutor and cognitive coach who manages the process rather than delivering content.
pitfall: Too little scaffolding, so novices flounder and misconceptions persist.
evidence: Mixed in school science; effective when strongly scaffolded (Hmelo-Silver, Duncan & Chinn, 2007).

name: Project-based science
distinct: Extended, artefact-producing work around a driving question.
teacher: Designs the driving question and scaffolds sustained inquiry.
learner: Investigator and producer of public artefacts.
pitfall: A product that can be completed without the science.
evidence: Promising results from well-designed curricula; outcomes vary with design and support.

name: Engineering design cycle
src: Various (for example, ask, imagine, plan, create, test, improve)
distinct: Success is a working solution, not an explanation.
teacher: Sets constraints and criteria, and coaches iteration.
learner: Designer who tests, fails and improves.
pitfall: Trial and error with no science used to justify design choices.
evidence: Integrated STEM evidence is varied; stronger when science concepts are explicitly required.

name: SSI-based teaching
distinct: Integrates values and ethics with scientific evidence.
fit: Genetics, Energy, Environmental sustainability, Data science 2.
teacher: Frames a contested issue, keeps the science sound, and facilitates respectful deliberation.
learner: Evaluates evidence and weighs values to reach a justified position.
pitfall: A debate built on opinion with thin science underneath.
evidence: Research shows gains in argumentation and reasoning; content gains vary.
